payload.throughline: Classify what the infectious particle contains, then trace how its information or conformation uses a host from entry through replication, assembly, release, transfer, or integration.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: identify one structure shared by enveloped and nonenveloped viruses. The packet declares no hard prerequisite; leaving the item blank records a nonconsequential abstention.
Goal: classify viruses by genome type, protein organization, envelope, phage structure, cellular absences, and relative size without memorizing a virus-family taxonomy.
A virion contains nucleic acid—DNA or RNA—inside a protein capsid. Some virions also carry a lipid envelope acquired from host membranes, with viral proteins embedded in it.
A bacteriophage can have a genome-containing head, tail, base plate, and fibers that attach to a bacterium and deliver the genome.

Viruses are acellular: they lack a nucleus, ribosomes, and energy-producing organelles, and cannot synthesize all components independently. Virions are much smaller than typical eukaryotic cells and usually smaller than bacteria.
Mental model: genome is the instructions, capsid is the package, envelope is an optional host-derived outer layer, and phage tail structures are delivery hardware.

Think aloud: if detergent destroys infectivity while the capsid remains, I infer an essential lipid envelope. If a diagram shows a head and tail fibers attached to a bacterium, I classify a phage and trace genome injection rather than whole-particle engulfment.
Worked example: a particle contains RNA, capsid proteins, and a lipid membrane but no ribosomes. It is an enveloped RNA virus, not a cell.
A head-tail particle binds a bacterial surface by fibers and delivers nucleic acid through its tail; that organization is bacteriophage structure.
Guided practice: sort each observed component into genome, capsid, optional envelope, phage delivery structure, or absent cellular machinery.
Less support: classify a fresh particle from one structural observation.
On your own: distinguish genome type and envelope status from a new component list.
Boundary: an envelope is not the capsid and is not universal. A virus does not become a cell because it carries nucleic acid, and a phage tail is not a flagellum for independent motility.
Near exit: classify a familiar virion from genome, capsid, and envelope evidence.
Changed-task exit: infer envelope dependence from detergent sensitivity rather than from a labeled diagram.
Repair the component function: every virus has genome plus capsid; only some have an outer lipid envelope. Keep genome type separate from envelope status.
Fresh near re-entry: classify a different genome-envelope combination with new options.
Repair the evidence function: detergent disrupts lipid layers. Loss of infectivity after detergent therefore supports an essential envelope, not the absence of a capsid.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: infer a structural feature from a different physical disruption.
Recap: viruses package DNA or RNA in capsid, may add an envelope, lack cellular machinery, and use specialized structures such as phage tails for host entry.
Starting check: identify why a virion cannot complete protein synthesis by itself. A blank response is an abstention, not an exit.
Goal: trace attachment and entry, use of host synthesis, component replication, assembly, and release in generalized phage or animal-virus cycles. Pathogenesis and treatment are outside scope.

Attachment begins when viral binding proteins recognize host surface molecules. Entry then delivers the genome or particle into the host; phages commonly inject genomes, while animal viruses may enter or fuse and then uncoat.
The viral genome directs production of nucleic acid and proteins using host energy, ribosomes, enzymes, or substrates, with details depending on genome type.
New genomes and structural proteins assemble into particles. Release can occur by host-cell lysis, budding, or another route appropriate to the virus.
Mental model: dock, deliver, copy and build, package, depart. Host dependence is concentrated in the copy-and-build stage but begins with compatible attachment.

Think aloud: if viral genomes and proteins accumulate separately but no infectious particles appear, synthesis succeeded and assembly is blocked. If no viral material enters after binding, the block is entry.
Worked example: a phage binds a bacterium, injects DNA, uses host machinery to make genomes and capsid proteins, assembles heads and tails, then releases particles after lysis.
An enveloped animal virus can acquire its membrane while budding from a host membrane during release.
Guided practice: place observation cards under dock, deliver, synthesize, assemble, or release.
Less support: identify one missing life-cycle stage from a host-cell observation.
On your own: order a fresh generalized cycle.

Boundary: assembly is not genome replication; it packages already made components. Attachment alone also does not establish entry, and budding is a release mechanism rather than the universal replication method.
Near exit: order generalized viral life-cycle stages.
Changed-task exit: localize a replication defect from measured genome, protein, and infectious-particle levels.
Repair the sequence function: group stages into host contact, information production, particle construction, and departure.
Fresh near re-entry: order a new subset with different stage wording.
Repair the localization function: detect the last successful output. Genome plus protein but no particles points after synthesis and before completed assembly.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: localize a different block using new entry-and-release data.
Recap: viruses attach, enter, use host resources to make genomes and proteins, assemble particles, and release them.
Starting check: identify the direction catalyzed by reverse transcriptase. No hard prerequisite is declared.

Goal: explain transduction and retroviral integration as distinct information-transfer mechanisms, and mark why prions and viroids do not fit those mechanisms. Clinical HIV treatment and a prion disease catalog are outside scope.
In transduction, a bacteriophage carries bacterial DNA from a donor bacterium to a recipient bacterium. The transferred DNA can then recombine or otherwise affect the recipient.
A retrovirus carries RNA. Reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from the viral RNA template, and viral DNA can integrate into a host chromosome as a provirus. HIV is a retrovirus example.

A prion is infectious protein without nucleic acid, so it does not transfer information by reverse transcription or DNA integration. A viroid is small naked RNA without a protein capsid and depends on host machinery but is not a retrovirus.
Mental model: transduction is phage delivery of bacterial DNA; retroviral integration is RNA → DNA → host chromosome.

Think aloud: if bacterial marker DNA appears in a recipient after a phage moves between cells, I choose transduction. If an RNA virus makes a DNA copy that inserts into a chromosome, I choose retroviral integration.
Worked example: a phage accidentally packages donor bacterial DNA and injects it into another bacterium. The bacterial gene transfer is transduction.
A retroviral RNA genome is copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase; integrase-mediated insertion produces a chromosomal provirus.
Guided practice: label the cargo, carrier, conversion enzyme, and final destination for each path.
Less support: identify a mechanism from one information-flow arrow.
On your own: distinguish transduction from integration and from subviral propagation.

Boundary: transduction is not ordinary phage genome replication; the transferred cargo is bacterial DNA. Reverse transcription is also not translation, and integration is not a property of protein-only prions.
Near exit: classify a familiar gene-transfer or integration scenario.
Changed-task exit: infer the missing enzyme from an RNA-to-chromosomal-DNA block.
Repair the mechanism function: identify cargo and destination. Bacterial DNA moved by phage is transduction; viral RNA converted to integrated DNA is retroviral integration.
Fresh near re-entry: classify a different donor-recipient scenario.
Repair the information-flow function: integration requires a DNA intermediate, so an RNA retrovirus must first use reverse transcriptase.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: use a new molecular observation to distinguish failure of reverse transcription from failure after DNA formation.
Recap: phages can transduce bacterial DNA; retroviruses reverse-transcribe RNA into DNA and integrate that DNA; prions and viroids follow neither full pathway.
Starting check: classify a protein-only infectious agent. A blank response remains a nonconsequential abstention.

Goal: distinguish viruses, prions, and viroids by composition and replication dependence while retaining transduction and retroviral integration as contrasts. Clinical HIV treatment and disease catalogs are outside scope.
A virus contains DNA or RNA enclosed by capsid and may have envelope. It uses host machinery to synthesize viral genomes and proteins.
A prion is infectious misfolded protein with no nucleic acid. It propagates by inducing a similar conformation in host proteins rather than by genome replication.

A viroid is a small naked RNA molecule without protein capsid. It relies on host processes for RNA replication and is distinct from a retrovirus because it does not form a capsid-containing retroviral particle or DNA integration pathway.
Mental model: virus = genome plus package; prion = protein shape; viroid = naked RNA.
Think aloud: nuclease-sensitive naked RNA with no capsid points to a viroid. Protease-sensitive infectivity with no detectable nucleic acid points to a prion. Capsid plus genome points to a virus.
Worked example: an infectious agent contains RNA inside protein capsid and produces particles in host cells. It is a virus.
A second agent contains no nucleic acid and propagates a misfolded protein conformation. It is a prion.
Guided practice: mark nucleic acid, capsid, protein-only propagation, and host dependence before choosing the entity.
Less support: classify a new agent from one composition test.
On your own: distinguish all three entities from a fresh evidence set.

Boundary: host dependence does not by itself identify a virus because viroids also depend on hosts. Nucleic acid alone also does not identify a virus because viroids contain RNA; capsid and composition complete the distinction.
Near exit: classify familiar virus, prion, and viroid descriptions.
Changed-task exit: combine nuclease, protease, and capsid evidence to classify an unknown agent.

Repair the composition function: ask two questions in order—Is nucleic acid present? Is a protein capsid present? Protein-only points to prion; naked RNA points to viroid; genome plus capsid points to virus.
Fresh near re-entry: classify a different entity using new composition wording.
Repair the perturbation function: nuclease targets nucleic acid, protease targets protein, and detergent targets lipid. Match lost infectivity to the agent’s essential material.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: classify a different unknown using another paired treatment result.
Recap: viruses package nucleic acid in capsid; prions propagate protein conformation without nucleic acid; viroids are naked host-dependent RNA.
